note: Rewritten from Light 1932 (revision of the American Amitermes), pp. 377—378; original in English; the morphology of the soldier and worker is described in the author's 1930 California monograph under the name A. wheeleri, and only the diagnostic characters and the alate measurements are given here; the material treated is a single dried specimen, so no range is given.

sections.label: Diagnostic characters
sections.text: The species is named for its small size: worker head width less than 0.8 mm, alate head width about equal to that of the worker, soldier head width less than 0.9 mm; the alate is only about 8.5 mm long including the wings. In 1932 the author separated it from A. wheeleri: the Texas specimens (Brownsville, San Antonio) and the alates previously assigned to A. wheeleri in the original description all belong to this species.

sections.label: Alate
sections.text: Described and figured by Snyder (1925): San Antonio, flying at 8:15 a.m. on 12 July (month 7, day 12); the author also had many individuals taken with a sweep net at Coachella, California, on 2 September (month 9, day 2), which agree closely with it. Measurements of one typical (dried) individual (mm): length including wings 7.50; forewing length 6.00; head length including the labrum 1.08; head capsule length 0.75; head width across the eyes 0.90; eye length 0.23; ocellus length 0.09; ocellus width 0.06; postclypeus length 0.22; postclypeus width 0.44; postclypeus index 0.50; pronotum length 0.48; pronotum width 0.78.

sections.label: Other
sections.text: The species does not build covered runways above ground, but constructs hard, crusty, often sand-covered galleries over wood lying on or buried in the ground, as do other members of the subgenus. It is more inclined than the other Californian species of the genus to attack standing timber, including fence posts and poles, and is the only local member of the genus that penetrates deep into the wood and is therefore the one most likely to be of economic importance. The original also notes that the severe damage reported by Snyder as caused by A. wheeleri cannot be accepted until it is established which species Banks actually had under that name.
